chapter: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk
title: Earl Hines, Ed Fox's Grand Terrace and Horace's 'Shufflin' Joe'
summary: Ed Fox owned the Grand Terrace with Hines and later Fletcher. Walter Fuller got Horace to arrange for Hines, whose band had Omer Simeon, Jimmy Mundy and George Dixon, as straw boss; Horace wrote 'Shufflin' Joe'. He sums up the varied bandleaders.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: : No, that's really true. Earl Hines is down here.

Father Hines. Let's see. That takes us back to Chicago, the Grand Terrace, where he used to play, aong with Fletcher, you know. There was a guy named Ed Fox that owned the Grand Terrace in Chicago that had Earl Hines under contract, and later on he had Fletcher under contract. And, of course, the original Grand Terrace nightclub first was located at 35th and Giles on the South Side of Chicago; they used to broadcast there, and they had entire revue reviews, with a line of 12 girls, comedians, shows there, like the Lilac Twelve Girls, (unintelligible) Dusty and tap dancers and all this stuff, like they had (unintelligible) Fletcher "Open the Door, Richard." "Fame." in this show,

And, of course, the Grand Terrace later moved up on 39th and South Park. This is where Count Basie was connected with the Grand Terrace, not the original one. But, nevertheless, getting back to Earl Hines, Earl had some great musicians

with him, like the great and late Omer Simeon, you know. That's the saxophone player that was in my band, and he was an excellent reader and later on he became famous for his dixieland work on clarinet. And I made a few arrangements for Earl because he was broadcasting like one of those same things in New York. And I was working in Chicago at the time, and I made quite a few things for him because the guys like Walter Fuller, who used to sing "Rosetta," would be featured in that band as a trumpet player, used to go to Earl and say, "Man, why don't you get little Smack to do some things for you, you know. And he says, "Little Smack writing?" one of those things. He said, "Well, have him come out and see me."
So I made a thing for him, and I called it "Shufflin' Joe," and I arrived at that title from Joe Louis, that did this shuffling, you know, with his feet in prize-fighting.

So it was a swinging thing, and those guys could play. And he had some great musicians in his band. In fact, a guy that was a great arranger, Jimmy Mundy, oh, man, and he had another trombone player. He had three trombonists -- another guy named Zilch, another guy named Al Wynn. Did you know Al Wynn? He was a real quiet fellow, but he was a very good musician. Of course, he had five saxophones. He had three trombones and three trumpets. He had a trumpet player that doubled on alto sax and

trumpet that I made some things for, and you should know this name, George Dixon. Well, Earl made quite a few records, and George did a lot of the solo work, and, of course, George was what they called, in again, bands in those days, he was the straw boss, you know. He took charge when Earl wasn't around. You know, and this was the nickname they label you with, like in Count Basie's band here a few years back when Marshall Royal was leading the band, they called him the straw boss, you know. So this is the title that is forced on you, whether you like it or not.

But Earl had a good band, and I made a few things for him, and he also was interested in originals. Seemed like so back in those days, all these guys had in mind that the original tunes would swing more, you know. I think this was the trend.
Well, they'd like to keep the book new and refreshed.

Yeah, that's it. And I think it is a fact that the originals last longer, you know, popularity wise, even if you get tired of playing them, and sometimes you can put them in the back of the book and let them rest for a few months, which they used to do, and then bring them out again, and they're fresh again, you know. And I think this is what they had in mind. But Earl was quite a guy. He's always been my favorite, you know, playing and sitting at the piano directing his band from there with finesse -- (unintelligible) also -- Father Hines. Fatha
Uh-huh. Well, that's quite an impressive list of people with whom you've worked.
It was quite an experience, for me, because the different band leaders on that list were so different.
-- Rubenoff, man. That was quite a thing, but they were all different, you know. And they'd put things in your mind that you'll never forget. You take them from now on right along with you.
